notes.b: Thermochemistry rests on one principle: energy is never lost, it only moves between the chemicals and their surroundings. Every energy calculation and explanation in this chapter relies on it.
points: Law of conservation of energy: energy cannot be created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another or transferred. This is why saying energy is 'used up' is wrong: it has gone somewhere else.

In a chemical reaction, chemical energy stored in bonds (the attractions that hold atoms together) is changed into, or comes from, other forms, mainly heat, but also light, sound and electrical energy.
Thermochemistry is the study of the heat changes that take place during chemical reactions and physical changes (changes of state, such as melting or boiling, where no new substance forms).
The system is the reacting chemicals; the surroundings are everything else, such as the solvent (the liquid the chemicals are dissolved in), container, air and thermometer.
Energy lost by the system is gained by the surroundings, and vice versa, so the total stays the same.

This law underpins all of thermochemistry: it is why the heat a reaction gives out can be measured as the heat gained by water, and why Hess's law (the rule for combining enthalpy changes of linked reactions) works. There is more on this in Hess's law.
notes.tip: If you are asked about energy in a reaction, say it is transferred or changed from one form to another. 'Energy is used up' is wrong.

notes.b: To compare the heat given out or taken in by different reactions, chemists need a measure of the energy stored in chemicals. That measure is enthalpy, and the quantity you actually use is the change in it.
points: Enthalpy (H) is the heat content, or stored energy, of a substance. It cannot be measured directly, but changes in it can.
The enthalpy change, ΔH, is the heat change in a process carried out at constant pressure (the pressure stays the same throughout): ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants).
The unit of ΔH is kJ mol⁻¹, meaning kJ per mole (the chemist's unit for an amount of substance) of reaction as written in the equation.

A negative ΔH means heat is given out to the surroundings (exothermic); a positive ΔH means heat is taken in (endothermic). There is more on this in the blocks on exothermic and endothermic reactions below.
Heat of reaction: the heat change when the numbers of moles of reactants shown in the balanced equation react completely.
notes.tip: Be ready to define heat of reaction: it is the heat change when the moles of reactants shown in the balanced equation react completely.

notes.b: Every reaction involves breaking bonds, so chemists measure how much energy a bond holds. That measure is bond enthalpy, and it tells you how strong a bond is.
points: Bond enthalpy: the energy needed to break one mole of a particular covalent bond (a bond in which atoms share electrons), with the molecules and the separated atoms all in the gaseous state.
Example: H₂(g) → 2H(g), ΔH = +436 kJ mol⁻¹, so the H–H bond enthalpy is 436 kJ mol⁻¹.
Bond enthalpies are always positive, because energy must always be supplied to break a bond.
The strength of the same type of bond varies slightly from one molecule to another, e.g. a C–H bond in methane and in ethanol, so tables give average bond enthalpies, averaged over many compounds.

The larger the bond enthalpy, the stronger the bond. The triple bond in nitrogen, N≡N (945 kJ mol⁻¹), is very strong, which is why nitrogen gas is so unreactive: a great deal of energy is needed to break it. There is more on this in ΔH from bond enthalpies.
notes.tip: Define bond enthalpy with the gaseous state included, because bond enthalpies refer to gaseous molecules and atoms. If asked why the N≡N (or C≡C) bond enthalpy is large, say the triple bond is very strong, so a lot of energy is needed to break it.

notes.b: A reaction is a swap of bonds: old ones in the reactants (the starting chemicals) are broken and new ones form in the products (the chemicals made). Whether heat is given out or taken in depends on which side of the swap involves more energy.
points: In a chemical reaction, bonds in the reactants are broken and new bonds are made in the products.
Bond breaking requires energy, so it is endothermic (it takes energy in).
Bond making releases energy, so it is exothermic (it gives energy out); forming a bond releases the same amount of energy as breaking it requires.
If more energy is released making the new bonds than is used breaking the old ones, the reaction is exothermic overall (the net result is heat given out) and ΔH is negative.
If more energy is needed to break bonds than is released making them, the reaction is endothermic overall and ΔH is positive.
Example: in H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g), one H–H bond and one Cl–Cl bond are broken and two H–Cl bonds are made.
The energy released forming the two strong H–Cl bonds is greater than the energy needed to break the reactant bonds, so the reaction is exothermic.

Example: in the combustion (burning in oxygen) of methane, the C–H and O=O bonds broken need less energy than is released forming the very strong C=O bonds in CO₂ and O–H bonds in H₂O, so combustion is strongly exothermic.
notes.tip: Bond breaking is never exothermic. 'Breaking bonds releases energy' is the commonest error. To explain in terms of bonds why a reaction is exothermic or endothermic, compare the energy needed to break the old bonds with the energy released making the new ones.

notes.h: Activation energy and the processes that transfer heat
notes.b: Even a reaction that gives out heat overall needs a push to get started, and the same bond balance explains the everyday processes the specification names.
points: Every reaction needs some energy to start breaking bonds, called the activation energy, even if it is exothermic overall. This is why a fuel such as methane does not burn until it is lit. There is more on this in Catalysis and energy profiles.

The processes the specification names all transfer energy as heat because of this balance of bond breaking and making: combustion, neutralisation (an acid reacting with a base), thermal decomposition (breaking a compound down by heating), rusting of iron, photosynthesis (plants making glucose using sunlight) and respiration (cells releasing energy from glucose).
Whether each one gives out or takes in heat depends on whether more energy is released making bonds or needed to break them.
notes.tip: Never say energy is used up when bonds are broken or made: it is transferred.

notes.h: Physical change also involves enthalpy change
notes.b: Energy changes are not limited to reactions. When a substance melts, boils or dissolves, no new substance forms, but heat is still taken in or given out.
points: Changes of state involve enthalpy changes because intermolecular forces (the weak attractions between separate molecules) are overcome or formed. Covalent bonds within the molecules are not broken.
Boiling water breaks the intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonds) between H₂O molecules, not the O–H covalent bonds inside each molecule, so the molecules stay intact as steam.
Melting, boiling and sublimation (solid changing straight to gas) are endothermic: energy is needed to overcome the forces between particles.
Water melting: H₂O(s) → H₂O(l), ΔH = +6.01 kJ mol⁻¹ (at 0 °C). Water boiling: H₂O(l) → H₂O(g), ΔH = +40.7 kJ mol⁻¹ at 100 °C.
Freezing and condensing are exothermic: the same amounts of energy are released as the forces form. This is why steam condensing on skin gives a severe burn.
Dissolving can be exothermic or endothermic. Dissolving sodium hydroxide or concentrated sulfuric acid in water gives out heat.
Dissolving ammonium nitrate takes in heat, which is used in instant cold packs.
Evaporation of sweat cools the body because the water takes in heat from the skin as it evaporates.
notes.tip: If asked why boiling water is endothermic, say energy is needed to overcome intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonds), and that O–H covalent bonds are not broken.

notes.b: Reactions are sorted by the direction of heat flow. The names, the sign of ΔH and the temperature change you can observe all tell the same story.
points: An exothermic reaction gives out heat to the surroundings; ΔH is negative and the products have less enthalpy than the reactants, because the system has lost heat.
An endothermic reaction takes in heat from the surroundings; ΔH is positive and the products have more enthalpy than the reactants, because the system has gained heat.
In an exothermic reaction in solution, the temperature of the mixture rises, so the container feels warm.
In an endothermic reaction in solution, the temperature falls, so the container feels cold, unless heat is being supplied continuously, as in thermal decomposition.

A thermochemical equation is a balanced equation with state symbols ((s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) dissolved in water) and the ΔH value, e.g. CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), ΔH = −890 kJ mol⁻¹.
State symbols matter because changes of state also have enthalpy changes.
Reversing a reaction reverses the sign of ΔH: if A → B has ΔH = −x, then B → A has ΔH = +x.

ΔH is proportional to the amounts in the equation, because twice as many moles react: doubling every coefficient (the number in front of each formula) doubles ΔH, e.g. 2CH₃OH(l) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 4H₂O(l), ΔH = −1452 kJ (2 × −726).
notes.tip: Exothermic means ΔH negative, not positive, because the system loses heat. In an endothermic reaction the surroundings get colder while the system gains heat. If asked for evidence that a reaction is exothermic, give the temperature rise.

notes.b: Many familiar processes give out heat. Learn the equation and ΔH for each of the named ones, and how to explain why each is exothermic.
points: Combustion: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), ΔH = −890 kJ mol⁻¹; all combustion reactions are exothermic.
Neutralisation: HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l), ΔH ≈ −57 kJ mol⁻¹. The ionic equation (showing only the ions that react) is H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l).
Respiration: C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) + 6O₂(g) → 6CO₂(g) + 6H₂O(l), ΔH ≈ −2800 kJ mol⁻¹; it releases energy in cells, which keeps warm-blooded animals warm.

Rusting of iron: iron reacts slowly with oxygen and water, which are both needed, to form hydrated iron(III) oxide (an oxide that has water combined with it). The simplified overall equation is 4Fe(s) + 3O₂(g) → 2Fe₂O₃(s), ΔH = −1648 kJ.
Rusting is exothermic, but the heat is released so slowly that it isn't noticed. Hand warmers use fast oxidation (reaction with oxygen) of iron powder to give out heat.
Other everyday exothermic processes: reactive metals reacting with acid or water, dissolving sodium hydroxide, condensing and freezing.
notes.tip: Rust is really hydrated iron(III) oxide, so the equation 4Fe(s) + 3O₂(g) → 2Fe₂O₃(s) is simplified, and rusting also needs water. When asked to classify a reaction such as combustion of methane or rusting of iron, give a reason.

notes.b: Endothermic changes take heat or light in from the surroundings. Some need heat supplied the whole time they run, which is why they only keep going while you keep heating.
points: Thermal decomposition: breaking down a compound by heating needs a continuous supply of heat, e.g. CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g), ΔH = +178 kJ mol⁻¹ (making lime).
Sodium hydrogencarbonate also decomposes endothermically: 2NaHCO₃(s) → Na₂CO₃(s) + H₂O(g) + CO₂(g), which is the reaction of baking powder in baking.
Photosynthesis: 6CO₂(g) + 6H₂O(l) → C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) + 6O₂(g), ΔH ≈ +2800 kJ mol⁻¹; the energy is absorbed from sunlight.
Photosynthesis and respiration are the reverse of each other, so their ΔH values are equal in size and opposite in sign.
Other endothermic processes: melting, boiling, dissolving ammonium nitrate (cold packs), and the reaction of citric acid with sodium hydrogencarbonate solution.
notes.tip: Do not give a ΔH value for the decomposition of NaHCO₃: it depends on whether the water is liquid or gas. For photosynthesis, state +2800 kJ mol⁻¹ because it is the reverse of respiration.

notes.h: Modelling energy transfer with enthalpy level diagrams
notes.b: A diagram shows at a glance whether a reaction gives out or takes in heat, and how much. There are two ways to draw the transfer.
points: An enthalpy level diagram has enthalpy (H) on the vertical axis, a horizontal line for the reactants and one for the products, and a vertical arrow between them labelled ΔH.
Exothermic: the products line is below the reactants line, the arrow points down, ΔH is negative, and the energy difference is released to the surroundings as heat.
Endothermic: the products line is above the reactants line, the arrow points up, ΔH is positive, and the energy difference is taken in from the surroundings.

A second way to model the transfer is a box containing the system, with arrows for heat flowing out to the surroundings (exothermic: the surroundings get warmer) or in from them (endothermic: the surroundings get cooler).

Diagram: two enthalpy level diagrams side by side: combustion of methane (CH₄ + 2O₂ above CO₂ + 2H₂O, ΔH = −890 kJ mol⁻¹, arrow down) and decomposition of calcium carbonate (CaO + CO₂ above CaCO₃, ΔH = +178 kJ mol⁻¹, arrow up).

Energy profile diagrams, which also show the activation energy (the energy needed to start the reaction) along the reaction pathway, are not needed here. There is more on this in Calculating ΔH and energy profiles.
notes.tip: When asked to draw an energy diagram, label the vertical axis enthalpy (H), name the reactants and products lines, and draw the ΔH arrow pointing down for exothermic and up for endothermic.

keyTerms.definition: The study of the heat changes that take place during chemical reactions and physical changes.
The law that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another or transferred.
The reacting chemicals in a thermochemical experiment.
Everything else outside the system, such as the solvent, container, air and thermometer.
The heat content, or stored energy, of a substance, which cannot be measured directly.
The heat change in a process carried out at constant pressure, in kJ mol⁻¹.
The energy needed to break one mole of a particular covalent bond with all substances in the gaseous state.
The heat change when the numbers of moles of reactants shown in the balanced equation react completely.
The minimum energy needed for a reaction to happen.
A reaction that gives out heat to the surroundings, with a negative ΔH.
A reaction that takes in heat from the surroundings, with a positive ΔH.
A balanced equation that includes state symbols and the ΔH value for the reaction as written.
A diagram with enthalpy on the vertical axis showing the reactant and product levels and the ΔH between them.
The breakdown of a compound by heating, which is endothermic and needs a continuous supply of heat.
The reaction of a substance with oxygen, giving out heat and usually light.
The reaction of an acid with a base, which is exothermic and forms water.
The release of energy from glucose in cells, which is exothermic.
The endothermic process in which plants use energy from sunlight to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water.

questions.prompt: Define bond enthalpy, and explain, in terms of the bonds broken and formed, why the reaction H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g) is exothermic.
questions.model: Bond enthalpy is the energy needed to break one mole of a particular covalent bond, with the molecules and the separated atoms all in the gaseous state. In the reaction, one H–H bond and one Cl–Cl bond are broken, which requires energy. Two H–Cl bonds are made, which releases energy. The energy released forming the two strong H–Cl bonds is greater than the energy needed to break the H–H and Cl–Cl bonds, so the reaction is exothermic and ΔH is negative.

questions.prompt: State the law of conservation of energy and explain how it applies when a reaction gives out heat.
questions.model: Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can only be changed from one form to another or transferred. When a reaction gives out heat, chemical energy stored in the bonds of the reactants is changed into heat. The heat lost by the system (the reacting chemicals) is gained by the surroundings (the solvent, container, air and thermometer), so the total energy stays the same.

questions.prompt: Explain why boiling water is endothermic, and why it does not involve breaking O–H bonds.
questions.model: Boiling water is endothermic because energy is needed to overcome the forces between the water molecules, the hydrogen bonds. Boiling changes H₂O(l) to H₂O(g), with ΔH = +40.7 kJ mol⁻¹ at 100 °C. The O–H covalent bonds within each molecule are not broken; only the intermolecular forces between molecules are overcome, so the water molecules themselves stay intact.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between exothermic and endothermic reactions and classify each of the following, giving a reason: combustion of methane; thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate; photosynthesis; rusting of iron.
questions.model: An exothermic reaction gives out heat to the surroundings, so ΔH is negative and the products have less enthalpy than the reactants. An endothermic reaction takes in heat from the surroundings, so ΔH is positive and the products have more enthalpy than the reactants. Combustion of methane is exothermic: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, ΔH = −890 kJ mol⁻¹, and all combustion reactions are exothermic. Thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate is endothermic: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂, ΔH = +178 kJ mol⁻¹, because heat must be supplied continuously to break it down. Photosynthesis is endothermic: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, ΔH ≈ +2800 kJ mol⁻¹, because energy is absorbed from sunlight. Rusting of iron is exothermic: 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃, ΔH = −1648 kJ, because heat is released as the iron is oxidised, though very slowly.

questions.prompt: Draw labelled enthalpy level diagrams for (i) the combustion of methane, ΔH = −890 kJ mol⁻¹, and (ii) the decomposition of calcium carbonate, ΔH = +178 kJ mol⁻¹.
questions.model: (i) Combustion of methane: draw a vertical axis labelled enthalpy (H). Draw a higher horizontal line labelled CH₄ + 2O₂ for the reactants and a lower line labelled CO₂ + 2H₂O for the products. Draw a vertical arrow between the lines pointing down, labelled ΔH = −890 kJ mol⁻¹, because the products are at lower enthalpy and heat is released. (ii) Decomposition of calcium carbonate: draw a vertical axis labelled enthalpy (H). Draw a lower horizontal line labelled CaCO₃ for the reactant and a higher line labelled CaO + CO₂ for the products. Draw a vertical arrow pointing up, labelled ΔH = +178 kJ mol⁻¹, because the products are at higher enthalpy and heat is taken in.

questions.prompt: Given that C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O has ΔH = −2800 kJ mol⁻¹, state ΔH for photosynthesis and explain.
questions.model: ΔH for photosynthesis is +2800 kJ mol⁻¹. Photosynthesis is the reverse of the reaction given, so its ΔH has the same size but the opposite sign. Photosynthesis is endothermic because energy is absorbed from sunlight.
